r: HTL 1010 pairs classroom instruction on hotel organizational structure with a hands-on shadowing component across front office, housekeeping, food and beverage, administration, and sales departments at the on-campus SpringHill Suites. The applied tasks map to O*NET activities spanning coordinating others' work, organizing and planning, and observing live departmental operations — a mix task-exposure research treats unevenly: the administrative overview content is moderately exposed, while the immersive shadowing across live hotel operations sits closer to low-exposure, presence-dependent categories. As a gateway course, it is also foundational scaffolding feeding at least four later required courses in this catalog set, which caps near-term erosion regardless of how automatable individual departmental content becomes. At 24 months, with limited hotel-industry AI diffusion and near-zero curricular restructuring, the instrumental need for this integrative, partly embodied orientation to the field is essentially intact.

By 2031, AI tools will plausibly draft departmental reports, summarize organizational structures, and answer orientation-style questions about how hotel functions interrelate, eroding the informational half of the course. Observed-usage data shows office and administrative-support tasks are already a substantial AI usage share, which pushes the base automatability of the lecture content upward. But the shadowing component still requires a student physically present across departments to build applied judgment, and the course's role as prerequisite substrate for casino management, resort operations, current-trends, and revenue-management coursework caps the erosion at Medium regardless of the horizon's diffusion level. The instrumental case shifts toward the experiential, in-person orientation the shadowing provides rather than the descriptive content, which increasingly can be AI-generated on demand well before the field-experience portion becomes similarly substitutable.

A decade out, AI orientation and training tools could plausibly generate detailed walkthroughs of hotel departmental structure and even simulate coordination scenarios, and the administrative-knowledge component of the course is substantially eroded under a central-capability-growth case. The foundational-scaffolding cap no longer binds at this horizon, and with no institutional or licensure lock protecting the course, the rating rises to High. The genuine hedge is the shadowing element: real-time observation of live departmental operations, staff coordination, and guest-facing workflows is a presence-dependent activity that resists full substitution even as capability grows, so some instrumental residue plausibly persists beyond what the pure rating implies. The wide ten-year uncertainty band applies with particular force to how much of this gateway course's content remains classroom-deliverable by AI versus requiring the shadowing experience.
HTL 1010.d: In this course, students integrate theoretical knowledge with practical experience, focusing on key areas in a hotel, such as front office, housekeeping, food and beverage, administration and leadership, and marketing and sales. Students explore the structure of hotel organizations, the functions of various departments, and how they collaborate to ensure smooth operations. In addition to lectures, students participate in a hands-on learning component, shadowing different departments at the on-campus SpringHill Suites at MSU Denver or similar hotel. This immersive approach helps students gain a comprehensive understanding of departmental roles and responsibilities while building essential skills for a successful career in hotel management.

r: Hotel Front Office covers the flow of business through a property — reservations, check-in, folio management, and settlement — with emphasis on planning and evaluating front-office operations within the broader hotel context. These tasks map to O*NET activities centered on interacting with computers, performing administrative processing, and communicating with guests, and property-management-system software already automates much of the transactional workflow the course describes. Observed-usage data shows office and administrative tasks are a leading AI usage category, pushing base exposure high even at this horizon. What keeps the rating from rising further near-term is the residual guest-facing service-recovery element and the limited diffusion of AI-native front-desk systems across the broader lodging industry to date. With no institutional lock on this course, the rating is Medium at 24 months, reflecting already-substantial but not yet complete erosion of the manual procedural content.

By 2031, self-service check-in, AI-assisted reservation systems, and automated night-audit and settlement processes will plausibly be standard across much of the industry, competently performing the transactional core this course teaches. Task-exposure research classifies routine administrative processing and system-based scheduling work among the more exposed categories, and diffusion of such tools in a data-forward industry like lodging is a reasonable central-case assumption by this horizon. No embodiment protection, foundational role, or accreditation lock caps the rating, so it rises to High: the applied front-office procedures the course's knowledge is put to are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most transactions. The residual is guest-facing exception handling and service recovery, real but a narrower slice of the course's procedural content than what erodes.

A decade out, AI-mediated guest interactions extend from booking through settlement are a plausible default across much of the lodging sector under a central capability-growth case, and the course's procedural and planning content is largely automatable. The rating holds High, with the residual competence concentrated in exception handling, VIP and complaint recovery, and evaluating front-office performance when systems misfire — narrower human tasks than the full front-desk-management curriculum this course currently teaches. No binding institutional or embodiment constraint holds the rating down at this horizon. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much in-person front-desk staffing the industry retains for brand and service-differentiation reasons even after the transactional work is fully automatable, a market question distinct from the instrumental necessity question this rating scores.
HTL 2512.d: This course examines hotel-front office procedures by detailing the flow of business through a hotel, from the reservations process to check-out and settlement. Students identify effective front- office management, with particular attention to the planning and evaluation of front-office operations. Front-office procedures and management are placed within the context of the overall operation of the hotel.

r: Casino and Gaming Management surveys the operational components of running a casino floor and sportsbook — accounting controls, games and gaming development, guest service, and industry career pathways. The content is predominantly analytical and discursive rather than embodied, mapping to O*NET activities in analyzing data, monitoring operational processes, and evaluating information against standards; accounting-control analysis in particular sits in a business-analytics category observed-usage data shows growing as an AI usage share. There is no accreditation or licensure lock specific to this survey course, and the guest-service component provides only modest protection since it is discussed rather than performed. At 24 months, with limited AI diffusion into casino-specific analytics and gaming-development workflows, the instrumental case is only partially eroded — AI can already summarize accounting controls and industry trends, but adoption inside the niche gaming-operations domain remains uneven. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI-assisted analytics for casino accounting controls, gaming-floor monitoring data, and sportsbook operations will plausibly be broadly deployed, and the descriptive and analytical content this course covers becomes substantially AI-deliverable. Task-exposure research places analytical and reporting work among the more exposed categories, and nothing in this course's structure — no embodiment, no institutional mandate, no foundational role for later coursework in this catalog set — caps the erosion. The rating rises to High: the applied operational-analysis tasks are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the course's content. The residual is guest-service judgment and floor-level real-time decision-making, genuine but a narrow slice of a course whose center of gravity is operational and accounting analysis rather than embodied service delivery.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most casino operational analytics, accounting-control review, and industry-trend synthesis competently, and the course's applied-knowledge content is substantially automatable. The rating holds High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how gaming-industry regulatory and compliance functions evolve — a regulated, cash-intensive sector could plausibly retain more human oversight than a pure capability read implies, even without a formal course-specific institutional lock. The residual instrumental value concentrates in real-time floor judgment and guest-service recovery, activities that remain outside the highest-exposure task categories. Confidence in this projection is moderate given the course's brief catalog description and the specialized, thinly evidenced nature of casino-industry AI diffusion relative to more heavily studied domains like general hospitality or retail.
HTL 2600.d: This course will allow students to analyze the key operational components of managing a casino floor and sportsbook. Accounting controls, games and gaming development, guest service, career opportunities, and the future of the casino industry will be explored.

r: Resort Operations examines the distinctive elements of managing and developing resort properties — recreational facilities, amenities, and service offerings — alongside environmental-impact analysis, planning and design considerations, and best practices for resort amenity and guest-service management. The course maps to O*NET activities in developing objectives and strategies, organizing and planning work, and analyzing data on environmental and operational impact — a planning-and-analysis profile similar to other business courses where observed-usage data shows planning-support tasks are a growing AI usage share. There is no institutional lock, and while guest-service management is discussed, the course is framed analytically rather than as embodied service delivery. At 24 months, with resort-specific AI diffusion still limited, the instrumental case for learning these planning and comparative-analysis frameworks is only partially eroded. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI planning-support tools will plausibly generate environmental-impact assessments, amenity-utilization analyses, and resort-development comparisons with facility, eroding much of the analytical content this course teaches. Task-exposure research classifies planning, synthesis, and comparative-analysis writing among more exposed activities, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint caps the rating for this upper-division elective. The rating rises to High: the applied planning and analytical tasks the course's knowledge serves are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most content. What plausibly persists is strategic judgment about capital-intensive resort development decisions and on-site guest-experience management, a narrower residue than the full comparative-analysis curriculum, consistent with how similar upper-division planning-oriented business electives are read at this horizon under current diffusion trends and observed adoption patterns in comparable knowledge-work domains.

A decade out, AI is plausibly embedded in resort planning and environmental-impact workflows as a default drafting and analysis tool, and the course's comparative and planning-analysis content is substantially automatable under a central capability-growth case. The rating holds High, hedged by the possibility that large-scale resort development decisions — carrying significant capital and environmental stakes — sustain more senior human judgment than a pure capability read implies. No binding institutional or embodiment constraint holds the rating down at this horizon. The wide ten-year uncertainty band applies to how resort-management education itself restructures around AI-generated planning drafts, not to whether the underlying comparative-analysis and design-consideration knowledge remains instrumentally distinctive at the level this course currently teaches it today, in this specific catalog context.
HTL 3500.d: Students in this course complete a comprehensive examination of resort operations, emphasizing the distinctive elements of managing and developing various types of resorts. Students explore the unique characteristics of resort properties, such as recreational facilities, amenities, and service offerings, and analyze how these differ from traditional hotels. Students gain a thorough understanding of the environmental impact of resort development, planning and design considerations, and best practices in managing resort amenities and guest services.

r: Hotel Housekeeping teaches management of housekeeping operations from a big-picture perspective down to technical details — inspection standards, department interrelation, and the balance of guest service and profitability. The applied competence is managing embodied back-of-house operations: inspecting rooms and linens, coordinating physical labor and scheduling, and making real-time quality judgments on the floor, activities mapping to O*NET categories of inspecting structures and materials and coordinating others' physical work — precisely the low-exposure, presence-dependent categories task-exposure research identifies as resistant. Some scheduling and inventory administration is exposed to AI, giving modest automatability, but the technical, hands-on core of quality inspection and physical-operations management is not. At 24 months the instrumental need to learn this embodied management competence is essentially untouched. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI tools will more capably handle housekeeping scheduling, inventory forecasting, and labor-cost analytics, meaningfully augmenting the administrative side of the role. That does not reach the embodied core the course builds: inspecting physical room and property condition, training staff in hands-on technique, and making real-time judgment calls about quality and guest-readiness. Verification of housekeeping quality requires a human physically present to assess it, and this in-person, physical-presence requirement is exactly the dampening factor that keeps the rating from rising with AI capability growth generally. Diffusion of AI into back-of-house physical operations management remains inherently limited by the embodied nature of the work itself. The rating stays Low: the administrative shell around housekeeping automates meaningfully, but the inspection-and-coordination competence the course centers on does not.

Even under an aggressive central-case capability scenario, a decade of AI advancement does not reach the embodied core of managing physical housekeeping operations — quality inspection, hands-on technique training, and real-time coordination of a labor-intensive, presence-dependent function. Robotics could plausibly automate some routine cleaning tasks by 2036, an adjacent trend, but the managerial competence this course teaches — assessing quality, coordinating people and physical workflows, and balancing service against profitability on the floor — remains a human, in-person activity. The rating holds Low with reasonable confidence: embodiment is the whole point of what distinguishes this course from purely administrative hotel-operations content, and nothing in the evidence base suggests AI substitutes for physically inspecting and managing a hotel's back-of-house operations within this horizon.
HTL 3522.d: This course demonstrates how to manage housekeeping operations in the hotel industry. Students study the management of direct housekeeping day-to-day operations from the big picture perspective down to technical details. This course examines the interrelation of hotel departments, and maximum guest service and profitability.

r: Hotel Property Management covers blueprint reading, building construction safety, utility requirements, and mechanical systems as they relate to managing a hospitality property. The applied competence maps to O*NET activities in inspecting equipment and structures and evaluating conditions against safety standards — technical facilities work where a wrong reading of a mechanical system or safety condition carries real physical and liability consequences, a high verification burden (F2) that a language model's fluent-sounding but unverified analysis does not resolve. Some blueprint interpretation and code lookup is exposed to AI, giving modest near-term automatability, but assessing actual building and mechanical condition requires a human on-site. With a single-sentence catalog description, task mapping here is somewhat generic. At 24 months the instrumental need for this verification-anchored technical competence is essentially intact. Rating Low.

By 2031, AI will more fluently explain mechanical-system principles, summarize building codes, and assist with preliminary blueprint interpretation, eroding some of the informational content. But diagnosing real utility and mechanical-system conditions in an actual hospitality property — and certifying that a structure meets safety requirements — is exactly the adversarial, non-obvious-failure verification work task-exposure research and the jagged-frontier evidence flag as resistant: a plausible-sounding but wrong safety assessment carries physical risk that mandates a trained human's judgment. No embodiment or foundational-scaffolding constraint is needed to hold the rating down; the verification-burden dampener alone keeps it at Low across the five-year horizon regardless of how capable AI becomes at generating explanatory content about mechanical systems and building codes in the abstract.

A decade out, AI diagnostic and building-information-modeling tools will plausibly assist with mechanical-system troubleshooting and code compliance more capably, and the informational core of the course is substantially eroded in isolation. But verifying that a hospitality property's physical infrastructure is actually safe and functional remains a human, on-site competence with real liability stakes, and this course's technical facilities-management content is read through that same verification lens even at the ten-year horizon. The rating holds Low, though confidence is limited by the course's minimal one-sentence catalog description, which constrains how precisely its applied tasks can be mapped to specific occupational activities. The central-case hedge is that AI increasingly assists the diagnostic process without yet being trusted to certify safety outcomes independently.
HTL 3652.d: In this course, students examine blueprint reading, building construction safety, utility requirements, and mechanical systems as they relate to managing a hospitality property.

r: Current Trends in Lodging Industry has students discuss, analyze, evaluate, and formulate solutions to current topics in lodging, supplemented by site visits and industry guest speakers. The applied work is discursive synthesis of trend information and solution formulation, mapping to O*NET activities in analyzing information and interpreting its meaning for others — a category task-exposure research finds AI already handles competently for well-documented industry topics, and observed-usage data shows research-and-writing synthesis is a leading usage category. The site visits and guest-speaker interactions provide a modest in-person residue, but the bulk of the course's graded work is analytical discussion rather than embodied practice. With no institutional lock and a foundational role limited to feeding into this course alone, the rating at 24 months is Medium, reflecting already-substantial exposure tempered by limited near-term diffusion.

By 2031, AI will plausibly synthesize current-industry-trends content, generate solution proposals, and summarize guest-speaker-style expert perspectives with considerable fluency, eroding the informational and discussion-preparation work this course assigns. Task-exposure research classifies synthesis and solution-formulation writing among the more exposed activities, and no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding factor caps the rating at this horizon. The rating rises to High: the applied discussion-and-analysis tasks the course's knowledge serves are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most content generation. What plausibly persists is the value of direct, in-person exposure to practitioners through guest speakers and site visits — an experiential residue distinct from, and smaller than, the analytical-synthesis work that increasingly can be AI-generated on demand well ahead of this horizon.

A decade out, AI industry-analysis tools will plausibly track and synthesize lodging-sector trends in real time with more currency and depth than a single course term, and the discussion-preparation rationale for the course is substantially eroded under a central capability-growth case. The rating holds High, with the hedge that direct engagement with practitioners and properties — the guest-speaker and site-visit components — retains a distinct experiential value the analytical-synthesis content does not. No binding institutional constraint holds the rating down at this horizon. The wide ten-year uncertainty band concerns how a "current trends" course is even structured when AI trend-tracking outpaces a semester's cadence, not whether the underlying analytical-synthesis skill remains the most exposed part of what the course currently teaches.
HTL 4000.d: In this course, students will discuss, analyze, evaluate, and formulate solutions to various current topics and trends taking place in the lodging industry. May include on-site visits to local hotels and will also include a variety of guest speakers from the lodging industry.

r: Revenue Management teaches the foundational metrics and definitions used throughout the lodging industry, has students analyze lodging data, interpret report outputs, and make strategic inferences, and explicitly prepares students for the Certification in Hotel Industry Analytics exam. This is quantitative business analytics — data interpretation, forecasting, and strategic inference — mapping to O*NET activities in analyzing data and interpreting information for others, precisely the category observed-usage data shows growing fastest as an AI usage share and where productivity research documents substantial speedups on report generation and analysis. There is no embodiment and no institutional lock; the CHIA credential is a voluntary industry certification, not an accreditation-mandated requirement. At 24 months the instrumental case is already materially eroded for routine analysis — AI competently interprets standard revenue reports — while strategic framing remains the near-term residue. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI revenue-management platforms will plausibly perform the great majority of the data analysis, report interpretation, and forecasting this course teaches, competently generating the strategic inferences students currently learn to derive manually. Task-exposure research and observed-usage data both place quantitative business analytics among the most exposed activities, and with no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint binding this fully digital, terminal elective, nothing caps the rating from rising. The rating reaches High: the applied revenue-analytics work is performed competently by AI with limited human input for most of the course's core content. The residual is high-level pricing-strategy judgment in ambiguous or unusual market conditions, real but a narrower slice of practice than the metrics-and-interpretation curriculum the course currently centers on teaching.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing essentially all routine revenue-management analytics — dynamic pricing, demand forecasting, channel optimization — with human revenue managers concentrated in strategic oversight and unusual-scenario judgment. The instrumental case for a course teaching the foundational metrics and manual-interpretation skills is substantially eroded; the knowledge shifts from an execution skill to a verification-and-oversight competence held by fewer practitioners. The rating is High, hedged by the possibility that competitive, high-stakes pricing decisions retain more human strategic involvement than a pure capability read suggests, and by the general ten-year forecasting uncertainty this evidence base carries. This is among the most exposed courses in the batch precisely because its content sits squarely in the highest-exposure quantitative-analytics task category.
HTL 4100.d: This course provides students with the foundational metrics and definitions that are used throughout the lodging industry. Students will analyze various types of lodging industry data, interpret the results of a variety of reports, and make strategic inferences based on their analyses. In addition, this course prepares students for the exam required to obtain the Certification in Hotel Industry Analytics (CHIA). This certification is recognized internationally by the lodging industry as a knowledge benchmark for revenue management.

r: Lodging Regulatory Environment prepares students to manage the legal environment of lodging and food-service industries through decision-making techniques and case-study analysis. The course is fully digital and analytical — evaluating compliance scenarios, reasoning through case studies, and interpreting regulatory information — mapping to O*NET activities in evaluating information against standards and making decisions and solving problems. Legal-analysis and regulatory-summary writing sit among more exposed task categories, and no clinical or licensure lock protects this course specifically, since it is a business-elective survey rather than a bar-accredited legal curriculum. At 24 months, with a brief catalog description and limited AI diffusion into lodging-specific regulatory-compliance workflows, the case-study critical-thinking component provides partial near-term protection against faster erosion, keeping realized automatability below its ceiling. Rating Medium.

By 2031, AI legal-research and compliance-summary tools will plausibly analyze regulatory case studies and draft decision-analysis memos with considerable fluency, eroding much of the case-study-preparation work this course assigns. Task-exposure research finds legal-document analysis and summary among more exposed activities even as science-adjacent critical-thinking work is comparatively protected; this course sits closer to the exposed pole given its emphasis on applying known regulatory frameworks rather than open-ended reasoning. With no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint binding, the rating rises to High: the applied regulatory-analysis tasks the course's knowledge serves are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most content. The residual is judgment on genuinely novel or contested compliance situations, a narrower slice than the case-study curriculum as currently taught.

A decade out, AI compliance-analysis tools will plausibly handle most routine regulatory interpretation and case-study reasoning for lodging and food-service operators, and the course's decision-making-technique content is substantially eroded under a central capability-growth case. The rating holds High, hedged by the jagged-frontier concern that a confidently wrong regulatory reading carries real legal and liability consequences, which could sustain more human verification of AI-generated compliance analysis than a pure exposure read implies. No binding institutional lock holds the rating down at this horizon. Confidence in this ten-year projection is moderate, constrained by the course's brief two-sentence catalog description, which limits how precisely its case-study content can be mapped against specific regulatory-domain occupational evidence and against the evidence palette's broader legal-reasoning and compliance-work findings.
HTL 4200.d: This course will help prepare students to effectively manage the ever-changing legal environment of the lodging and food-service industries. Decision-making techniques will be introduced to allow students to demonstrate effective critical thinking in case study analyses and exercises.

r: Applied Hotel Management is a capstone in which students use simulation software to manage a hotel within a simulated competitive market, making executive-level decisions across market share, revenue optimization, forecasting, capital investment, channel management, and food-and-beverage revenue sourcing. This is fully digital, quantitative strategic decision-making, mapping to O*NET activities in developing objectives and strategies and analyzing data — a profile closely resembling other capstone business-strategy courses where AI already competently drafts financial forecasts and scenario analyses, and observed-usage data shows business-planning tasks are a substantial and growing AI usage share. There is no embodiment or institutional lock, and as a terminal capstone it scaffolds no later required course. At 24 months, with the simulation environment already partially AI-assistable, the rating is Medium, reflecting substantial near-term exposure in a course with no protective structural factor.

By 2031, AI decision-support tools will plausibly generate the forecasting models, capital-investment analyses, and channel-management strategies this simulation-based capstone has students produce manually, competently performing the great majority of the quantitative strategic-planning work. Task-exposure research and productivity studies both find business-planning and financial-analysis tasks among the more exposed and AI-augmentable activities, and with no embodiment, licensure, or foundational-scaffolding constraint protecting this terminal course, the rating rises to High. The applied executive-decision tasks the course's knowledge serves are performed competently by AI with limited human input for most scenarios. The residual is integrative executive judgment under simulated competitive uncertainty — synthesizing across departments and betting on a strategy — a real but narrower competence than the full quantitative-planning curriculum this capstone currently builds.

A decade out, the central case has AI performing most of the quantitative strategic-planning work this capstone teaches — forecasting, revenue optimization, capital-investment modeling — with human involvement concentrated in final integrative judgment and accountability for the chosen strategy. The instrumental case for a course centered on manually producing these analyses is substantially eroded; the competence shifts toward directing and validating AI-generated strategic recommendations rather than building them from scratch. The rating is High, hedged by the possibility that executive-level strategic judgment under genuine uncertainty retains more human weight than a pure capability read implies, and by general ten-year forecasting uncertainty. As a capstone synthesizing already-exposed quantitative business tasks, this course tracks toward the more exposed end of the hospitality-management catalog.
HTL 4500.d: This course will focus on the business decisions made at the management and executive levels of a hotel and how those decisions affect not only the property itself but also a hotel's competitive set. A real market dynamic is simulated for a hotel that students will manage, with a focus on the financial results of key areas such as market share, revenue optimization, forecasting, capital investment, channel management, and food & beverage revenue sourcing. Utilizing simulation software, students will develop a competitive and operational strategy, implement the strategy, and review the results of their decisions in a simulated market environment.
